Actionable next steps include asset sharing, editing timeline, and publishing plan.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-12-03 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE); Aisha Malik (Redwood Content Lead); Samantha Lee (BrightWave CMO); Carlos Rivera (BrightWave Head of Product); Dina Patel (BrightWave Eng)
Recording: zoom/recording/link (internal)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Jordan from Redwood, and we are super excited to have BrightWave on to talk about how you all are using Redwood Inference. Aisha, you're co-hosting — do you wanna intro the flow?
[00:18] Aisha: Yeah, hi hi, thanks, Samantha and team for making time. We'll keep this informal, chat through the background, the technical bits that are interesting to our audience, then talk outcomes and a few anecdotes. If it's okay, we'll record and then share the edited version for your sign-off.
[00:34] Samantha: Sounds great. Happy to. We love your product and excited to tell the story.
[00:38] Jordan: Awesome. To start, can you give a quick primer — what prompted BrightWave to look for an inference platform?
[00:45] Samantha: Sure. So our marketing personalization stack had an increase in real-time generation requests — chat and subject line generation — and our costs were spiking plus latency was inconsistent. We were juggling between a self-hosted open model infra team and some managed APIs, and it was pretty messy. We were looking for something that would give us predictability and better unit economics but without handing over the keys entirely.
[01:10] Carlos: Adding on, we also had a hard requirement for some features: SSO/SAML integration for the console, audit logs for compliance, and ability to run in a VPC for certain sensitive campaigns. Latency under 200ms for inference tail was a stretch for our previous setup.
[01:28] Jordan: That aligns a lot with other customers. When you evaluated, what were the main tradeoffs you considered — hosted Redwood vs dedicated vs private?
[01:36] Samantha: We did a cost analysis. Hosted got us off the ground fastest, but for peak traffic and PII workflows we needed isolation. We ended up going with Dedicated for most traffic and Private for a few pilot campaigns that required on-prem-like controls. Also, the Redwood team helped with benchmarks which made the decision easier.
[01:55] Aisha: Did you run any baseline benchmarks — can you share a quick number on latency and cost delta?
[02:02] Dina: Yeah, our engineers ran a 99th percentile tail latency test over a week. On our previous infra the p99 for 512-token prompts was ~520ms, with Redwood Dedicated after tuning batching and KV-cache we were seeing p99 ~170-190ms. Cost per token dropped roughly 30% after enabling prefix caching and switching to a quantized variant for lower-critical calls.
[02:29] Jordan: Nice, that's great to hear. A lot of listeners care about the tuning story — what was the ramp like from onboarding to production?
[02:37] Carlos: It was surprisingly smooth. SE worked with us on model selection and quantization profiles, and we ran a short POC for two weeks. There were a couple of hiccups: one around our request shaping which initially caused some tokenization mismatch — the transcript is a little fuzzy there but essentially we had to normalize newline handling — but SE helped patch our client stub.
[03:00] Samantha: From a product perspective, the Redwood Console dashboards were useful — we could see token cost, per-route latency, which helped prioritize routes to optimize first.
[03:12] Aisha: On the security side, did you have any concerns during procurement? I know many customers ask about SOC 2, KMS, audit logs.
[03:20] Dina: We required SOC 2 plus KMS integration for key management. Redwood provided the security pack and a short SOC 2 attestation doc; we also insisted on customer-managed keys for some data, which Redwood supported through their KMS integrations. There was some doc back-and-forth with legal but overall straightforward.
[03:38] Jordan: Good to hear. For the marketing angle, any favorite anecdotes or wins you can share?
[03:45] Samantha: Sure — one quick win: we launched a holiday subject-line A/B test using Redwood's generation endpoint and saw a 7% uplift in opens. That was a clear marketing win we could tie to lower cost and faster iteration. Another was reducing manual copy review time because generated drafts were higher quality after model and prompt tuning.
[04:07] Aisha: Love that. Anything surprising or unexpected?
[04:10] Carlos: The surprise for us was how much savings came from prefix caching — we had many repeated starts for our templates and enabling caching cut a lot of redundant compute. We didn't realize our traffic shape would benefit so much.
[04:24] Samantha: And the support team — we did a late-night deploy during a campaign and SE was on the call, which was clutch.
[04:33] Jordan: That's the kind of story marketing folks like. Switching gears, listeners will want some technical flavor — do you want to talk briefly about the private deployment experience?
[04:42] Dina: Sure. For our private deployments we used Redwood Private in our AWS VPC. The install was mostly containerized. We had to open a few subnets, and there was one kernel-level optimization that the infra team suggested to get better throughput on our instance types — again some terminology got fuzzy in the auto transcript, but basically it was about selecting the right quantized kernels and disabling transparent hugepages for better latency stability. Redwood's SE helped with a custom kernel param set.
[05:10] Jordan: Nice detail. Did you ever consider fully self-hosting an open-source runtime and doing the orchestration yourselves?
[05:17] Carlos: We did a cost/ops analysis. The initial engineering effort to match Redwood's runtime optimizations and orchestration was significant. For scale and the features we wanted (tracing hooks, rollouts, automatic fallbacks), Redwood's offering made sense given the speed to market.
[05:33] Aisha: One thing marketing will want to highlight is team workflow — how are marketing, product, and engineering collaborating on prompt changes and model rollouts?
[05:40] Samantha: We use a shared spreadsheet + PR-style review for prompt sets. Engineering exposes a staging route in Redwood and product/marketing test changes there. When it's stable, we do a canary rollout via the console. That process reduced friction and sped up iteration.
[05:58] Jordan: Good operational pattern. Quick question — any concerns about vendor lock-in or portability?
[06:05] Carlos: We were mindful. Redwood supports pinning model versions and exporting prompts; also they provide an export of KV data and logs which helps. We still keep a small self-hosted fallback for emergency, but it's more of a contingency than mainline.
[06:20] Aisha: For the podcast, do you have any favorite quote or soundbite you want us to use?
[06:25] Samantha: Maybe: "Redwood let us move from experimentation to predictable personalization — faster tests, better opens, and lower bills."
[06:34] Jordan: Love that. We'll flag it for the editor.
[06:38] Aisha: We should also capture a quick technical pull-quote — Carlos?
[06:41] Carlos: "Prefix caching was the unexpected 30% win for us."
[06:45] Jordan: Perfect. We'll include both as pull-quotes.
[06:48] Samantha: One editorial note — please don't publish internal campaign numbers beyond the 7% uplift. Keep site metric references high-level.
[06:55] Aisha: Understood. We'll anonymize details.
[06:58] Jordan: Great. Any final comments on onboarding or advice for other teams?
[07:03] Dina: My advice is instrument early. The Redwood Console made it obvious where to optimize; capturing latency and cost per route is key.
[07:12] Samantha: And involve marketing early in prompt strategy — saves time later.
[07:17] Jordan: Excellent. We'll wrap with logistics. Next steps: we'll send raw audio + transcript to you by the 10th, ask for headshot/bio by the 9th, schedule a 30-minute edit review on 2025-12-12. Anything else?
[07:33] Samantha: No, that covers it. Thanks everyone — excited to see the final piece.
[07:38] Jordan: Thanks all. Aisha, we'll loop in your team for the edit.
[07:42] Aisha: Yep. Bye everyone.
[07:44] (meeting ends)

Notes: Transcript includes occasional auto-transcription errors (e.g., K-V cash for KV cache, kernel param phrases). Shared artifacts referenced: redwood-case-study-deck.pdf (link), benchmark-spreadsheet.xlsx (link), raw audio file (link).
